findings.claim: FileStore::write joins an attacker-controlled key onto the store root with no sanitization or canonicalization, giving an attacker an arbitrary-file-write primitive with attacker-chosen contents outside the store root. A key of "../../.ssh/authorized_keys" (or, on Windows, an absolute key like "C:\\Windows\\Temp\\evil.bat", since Path::join replaces the base when the argument is absolute) writes anywhere the process can reach; the fs::create_dir_all(parent) on line 33 additionally lets the attacker create arbitrary directory trees before the write. No control exists anywhere in the crate: no sanitization at the caller, no canonicalize()/starts_with(root) check, and the key is a bare &str with no constraining type.
findings.proposedReproduction: let s = FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into())?; s.write("../../../tmp/pwned", b"x")?; assert!(std::path::Path::new("/tmp/pwned").exists()) — file created outside the store root.

findings.claim: FileStore::read joins an attacker-controlled key onto the store root without sanitization (line 26), so a key of "../../secret" or "..\\..\\secret" resolves outside the root and fs::read returns the contents to the caller — arbitrary file disclosure limited only by process file permissions. Because Path::join replaces the base for an absolute argument, a key of "/etc/passwd" reads that file directly with no traversal segments at all. The doc comment on line 22 states keys arrive from the wire untrusted, and FileStore is re-exported publicly from lib.rs line 12, so the untrusted key reaches the join by the crate's own documented contract. status_response (lines 39-44) is a second reachable sink for the same primitive, and it leaks the outcome back in API terms, confirming existence of out-of-root paths via the Ok/Error discriminant even when bytes are not returned.
findings.proposedReproduction: let s = FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into())?; s.read("../../etc/passwd") returns the contents of /etc/passwd rather than an error.

findings.claim: handle_request calls unwrap() on attacker-controlled request parsing (lines 28-29), letting any unauthenticated peer terminate request handling with a single malformed message. The request "put" panics on the missing-key unwrap, "put:k" panics on the missing-TTL unwrap, and "put:k:notanumber" panics on parse().unwrap(). This is an attacker capability rather than a mere crash because SPEC.md requirement 2 makes non-termination the control: malformed input must produce an error response and must never terminate the process. The get arm on lines 18-24 handles a missing argument correctly, showing the safe pattern was available and simply not applied to the put arm.
findings.proposedReproduction: handle_request(&mut cache, "put") panics at api.rs:28 instead of returning Response::Error.

findings.claim: SharedCounter::read_or_init drops and re-takes the lock between the contains_key check (line 83) and the get().unwrap() (line 84), so a concurrent remove() lands in the window and the unwrap panics. The security-relevant escalation is that this panic occurs while the temporary MutexGuard from line 84 is still alive, which poisons the inner Mutex permanently; every subsequent lock().unwrap() in read_or_init and remove then panics unconditionally. A transient race an attacker can drive by interleaving counter reads and removes for the same key is therefore converted into permanent, unrecoverable denial of service for the entire counter subsystem, persisting for the life of the process with no recovery path since no call site handles the PoisonError.
findings.proposedReproduction: Spawn a thread looping counter.remove("k") against a thread looping counter.read_or_init("k"); after the panic at cache.rs:84, all later read_or_init calls panic on the poisoned lock at cache.rs:83.
